headline: 50+ DEATHS. $1B.
**72 HOURS** TO FLAG
cover.hook_pick_reason: The hook judge scored the number hook highest: three hard figures, readable at a glance. Slide 2 delivers the 50 deaths and $1B trigger and slide 5 delivers the 72 hours; "to flag" matches evaluators notifying Commerce, so it does not overclaim. The "brake" hook had no number or name. Option 3 overclaims lab attitudes.
cover.image_prompt: Cinematic shot of a giant steel emergency lever mounted on a monumental dark server wall, a single beam of cold light across it, glowing data corridors fading into haze behind. Main subject in the upper half, lower third in shadow. No text, no letters, no logos, no people.

slides.title: Anthropic pitches a safety bill
body: Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI models, circulated a **draft federal bill**, Politico reported. It is not introduced legislation. Anthropic hopes Congress will consider it.

slides.title: When a model could be blocked
body: A release could be halted over a "foreseeable, imminent risk" of **over 50 deaths** or **over $1 billion** in property damage.

slides.title: Three kinds of danger
body: Qualifying risks are a **biological weapon**, a model **evading its developer's controls**, or a cyberattack. The thresholds resemble California's SB 53, now law.

slides.title: Outside evaluators, then a judge
body: Independent evaluators would register with the **U.S. Commerce Department**, the federal agency that oversees trade. Labs could pay them only if payment is not contingent on their results.

slides.title: 72 hours, then a D.C. court
body: After finding an imminent risk, evaluators would have **72 hours** to notify Commerce, which would ask a D.C. judge to halt the release. Federal agencies could not halt distribution on their own discretion.

slides.title: Not everyone wants new rules
body: Labs have mostly resisted mandatory oversight. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argues **no new laws are needed**.

facts.text: Anthropic circulated a draft federal AI safety bill, per Politico; it is a draft Anthropic hopes Congress will consider, not introduced legislation.
The block trigger is a "foreseeable, imminent risk" of over 50 deaths or over $1 billion in property damage.
Qualifying risks are a biological weapon, a model evading its developer's controls, or a cyberattack. The thresholds resemble California's SB 53, now law.
Independent evaluators would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department and payable by labs only if payment is not contingent on their results.
After finding an imminent risk, evaluators have 72 hours to notify Commerce, which would ask a D.C. judge to halt the release. Federal agencies could not halt distribution on their own discretion.
Labs have mostly resisted mandatory oversight; Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argues no new laws are needed (paraphrase).

sources.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed

caption:
An AI lab just drafted the rules that could stop its own models.

Anthropic circulated a draft federal AI safety bill, Politico reported. It is a draft, not introduced legislation.

→ Trigger: a "foreseeable, imminent risk" of over 50 deaths or over $1 billion in damage
→ Independent evaluators have 72 hours to notify the Commerce Department
→ Commerce would then ask a D.C. judge to halt the release

Should AI labs help write the rules that govern them?

Source: TechCrunch (citing Politico), Oct 20, 2026.
